name: Division No. 1

storage_detail.nearest_well: Core Energy Otsego County EOR Operations

rationale: Diffuse wet animal manure / biosolids, low nutrient status, poor geologic storage access (no affordable route to a storage well) -> wet feedstock far from affordable geologic storage favors hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) to a stable bio-crude (~50% CDR efficiency): it handles the wet biomass without drying and densifies the carbon for haulage to a distant well. Pricier than direct injection, so used only where storage is distant.
caveats: Transport to the nearest well exceeds $100/tCO₂ for this pathway's payload — defaulted to a storage-independent option or densified bio-oil.

ranked.label: Bio-oil (hydrothermal liquefaction)
pros: Handles WET biomass (manure/biosolids) directly — no drying needed
Hydrothermal liquefaction densifies the carbon into a stable bio-crude, cheap to haul to distant wells
Viable where wet-slurry injection/AD would need nearby geologic storage
Suits the region's diffuse, distributed biomass
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$116/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
Higher cost and earlier-stage than pyrolysis or direct injection
Lower CDR efficiency than slurry injection (~50% vs >90%)

ranked.label: Biomass waste injection
pros: Very high CDR efficiency (>90%)
Cheaper on balance than bio-oil where wells are near
PFAS destruction; disposes problematic wet wastes
cons: Transport to the nearest operating well ~$673/tCO₂ — exceeds the $100/tCO₂ viability cap, so this pathway is not viable here
No emissions-avoiding co-product
Hauling bulky, less-carbon-dense biomass is costly if wells are far
Geologic storage is poor/absent here — a major constraint
